commenti.body: I'd love to read up on animation history. Any time, any place. Popular or academic books would both be welcome!

I recently re-watched Mad Max Fury Road and my *GOD* that is a great movie. It is so entertaining in every aspect. Perfectly paced. Each character feels so unique with only quick introduction. And of course, the spectacle of it is immense, especially knowing that all of those stunts were performed for real on camera. The cars and rigs were all real, and they were really driving. Incredible.

I haven't seen Road Warrior or Thunderdome in something like 30 years? I barely remember anything about them, but I think I might need to rewatch them too, and then see if I can track down a copy of the Blood and Chrome edition of Fury Road. If anyone has any thoughts on that edition I'd love to hear them. Fury Road has such vivid and beautiful color, even the very obvious blue-light filter over the night scenes (save for very specific instances of diagetic light, which is very cool). So I wonder how well it works in Black and White.

I wrote a review for "Cure". It's been a favorite of mine for about a year, and I finally wrote a review for it, only after seeing again in 35mm. Also, I wrote a review of Bresson's "Lancelot du Lac" which is also on my Letterboxd. Feedback is more than welcome :)

I've actually read quite a bit about this. My recommendations:

*Hollywood Cartoons: American Animation in Its Golden Age* by Michael Barrier

*Walt Disney's Nine Old Men and the Art of Animation* by John Canemaker

*On Disney by Sergei Eisenstein* (yes, **that** Sergei Eisenstein) 

*Enchanted Drawings: The History of Animation* by Charles Solomon

*Chuck Amuck: The Life and Times of an Animated Cartoonist* by Chuck Jones
Thanks! Funnily enough, the Eisenstein is the only one of these I've read already :)

No country for old men has reached a new hight for me.   

 on my most recent rewatch I had it on in the living room screen and without subtitles (English is my second language) and my roommate who is film illiterate came in a third of the way through and he sat down and pulled his phone and when the hotel Scene came up he was somewhat interested and after a few minutes he was hooked even though he couldn't understand a word of it so I asked him if he's interested enough I could pull-up subtitles but he didn't want to inconvenience me and said no.   
I tried anyway even though Half-heartedly but it was too much work and I gave up and by the end of the film he was completely mesmerized by it. Two days after he asked me about the name of the film so he could watch it on his own.    

The efficiency of the visual story telling in this film is just top tier,  show don't tell indeed.

Curious if anyone here might know how the U.S. National Film Registry actually preserves movies. Their FAQ says that the NFR "seeks to ensure that a selected title either has already been preserved or will be in the future," working with "motion picture studios, independent filmmakers, archives, museums and historical societies." That makes it sound like there's no big archive room at the Library of Congress with film canisters or hard drives containing the actual films on the Registry. So functionally, what happens when a film is placed on the Registry in terms of preservation for the future?
I recently did a re-watch as well. Two things to add: amazing soundtrack, lots of themes to analyze that one might miss because of all the spectacle (basically it's not just a cool action flick)

I watched Past Lives and I just don't get the hype at all. It was one of the weakest movies I've watched this year and if I didn't know it was the director's debut I would've assumed so. She basically just copied her own life story hoping it would translate well onto screen but to me it all just felt incredibly slow, inauthentic and vacuous. 

I found the writing in particular to be weak. The dialogue felt unrealistic and stale, we barely got a deeper look into the characters (esp. the Korean male protagonist) that would help the audience understand why they act the way they do, and most disappointing is the fact that the director taps into the same old tropes and narratives about Asians despite her own heritage.

I remember someone recommending a Japanese movie about former students visiting their professor. Does anyone know what movie it could be? I think they described it as a comedy/drama. As for director, I think it's a well-known one like Kurosawa, but I can't remember the name.

I agree, I think it went into the worst tropes about autofiction. Completely blank slate protagonist, nonexistant story and stakes, just thoroughly uninteresting narrative and pretty blandly made as well. People compare it to Lost in Translation, but just the sheer disparity in the quality of the filmmaking should just put that to rest immediately

I would not say it is the worst BUT it does have fit someone who is still a neophyte.

​

 The film story leaves a lot to be desired. It definitely feels like almost entirely different to my family's  immigrant experience. I would not say that my other family did not acclimatize with the American culture like the film's protagonist BUT there is something about it that feels untrue even though its looking in about the same issue of 'otherness' of immigrant. 

I also hated how conflict averse it is. I think it was trying to get into that 2000s indie. Shocked by the acclaim.
